scenarios.title: An imported note cannot pose as the admin
scenarios.what: A note exported from another server claims it was written by 'boss'. After import it is stamped with the importer, flagged as unverified, and the claim is only a claim.

scenarios.title: Distrusting a claimed writer hides their imported note
scenarios.what: An unverified import claims it came from Mallory. Putting Mallory on the distrust list hides it, because claimed names count as taint.

scenarios.title: Both disputing writers distrusted: no answer rather than a wrong one
scenarios.what: If every source of an answer is distrusted, searches return nothing; they must not fall back to showing either side.

scenarios.title: A distrusted writer cannot replace a trusted note
scenarios.what: Replacing hides the original, so a writer the admin does not trust may not do it on their own.

scenarios.title: A less sure replacement needs an admin
scenarios.what: A new note that claims lower confidence than the one it would hide must not be able to hide it without an admin.

scenarios.title: An admin can accept the red flag, but only on purpose
scenarios.what: For a less sure replacement, even an admin must say they accept the risk. Without that, the confirm is refused.

scenarios.title: The warning names notes written by other people
scenarios.what: If a replacement hides someone else's note, the warning says so.

scenarios.title: Restoring an earlier version makes a new version
scenarios.what: Restoring does not erase anything: the text it replaces goes into the history too.

scenarios.title: A version by a distrusted writer cannot be restored
scenarios.what: Putting text back by an untrusted writer would launder it, so restore refuses.

scenarios.title: Only an admin can read a note's history
scenarios.what: Old text can hold what someone took out on purpose, so a normal writer cannot read it or restore from it.

scenarios.title: A restore made on an out-of-date copy is refused
scenarios.what: Restoring uses the same compare-and-swap rule as editing.

scenarios.title: A code made for one person is useless to another
scenarios.what: Alice's confirmation code must not work for Mallory, even though both can write.

scenarios.title: Only the editor chain shows in history, with writers
scenarios.what: The history names who wrote each earlier version.

scenarios.title: A plain writer cannot undo an admin's replacement
scenarios.what: An admin hides a bad note by replacing it. The bad note's own writer must not be able to bring it back; only an admin can.

scenarios.title: Reading another tenant's note by id
scenarios.what: Tenant B asks for tenant A's note by its id. It must look like the note does not exist. Tenant A can still read it.

scenarios.title: Writing into another tenant by naming it in the request
scenarios.what: Tenant B sends a note claiming namespace tenantA. The server must file it under tenant B and ignore the claim.

scenarios.title: Updating another tenant's note by id
scenarios.what: Tenant B tries to rewrite tenant A's note. Refused as 'not found', and the note is unchanged.

scenarios.title: Deleting another tenant's note by id
scenarios.what: Tenant B's admin tries to delete tenant A's note. Refused, and the note survives.

scenarios.title: Searching for another tenant's secret
scenarios.what: Tenant B searches for words only tenant A's note has, with and without naming tenantA as the namespace.

scenarios.title: Listing another tenant's notes
scenarios.what: Tenant B lists notes, asking for tenantA. Only tenant B's own notes may appear.

scenarios.title: Full export stays inside the tenant
scenarios.what: Each tenant's admin exports everything they may see. Each export has its own tenant's text and none of the other's.

scenarios.title: Importing cannot plant notes in another tenant
scenarios.what: Tenant B's admin imports a file whose notes claim namespace tenantA. They must land in tenant B; tenant A sees nothing new.

scenarios.title: Token downgrade: each scope gets exactly its own actions
scenarios.what: The same agent holds a read token, a write token and an admin token. Read can search but not write; write can write but not delete, export or import; admin can do all of it.

scenarios.title: Asking for hidden notes is admin-only
scenarios.what: include_distrusted switches the trust list off. A write token must be refused; a pinned admin gets only its own tenant's hidden notes.

scenarios.title: Trust rules of another tenant cannot be written
scenarios.what: Tenant B's admin tries to distrust a writer inside tenant A (and globally with '*'). Refused. Tenant A's note stays visible.

scenarios.title: A read grant lets B read A, never write
scenarios.what: The operator grants tenant B read access to tenant A. B may search A's notes; B may not edit or delete them; A still cannot read B.

scenarios.title: Signed export from tenant A, imported by tenant B's admin
scenarios.what: Tenant A's admin exports with signatures. Tenant B's admin imports it into B. The notes land in B, are flagged unverified, and B's admin cannot make the server believe A's signing key (that list is server-wide).

scenarios.title: Import can be told to reject unsigned notes
scenarios.what: With require_attestation, a file with no valid signatures is refused or yields nothing: no note enters the tenant.

scenarios.title: The 'what is relevant to this message' lookup stays in the tenant
scenarios.what: Tenant B sends a message full of tenant A's words. Nothing of A's may come back.

scenarios.title: The change feed stays in the tenant
scenarios.what: Tenant B's admin reads the feed of recent changes. Tenant A's titles must not be in it.

scenarios.title: Documented limit: a token with no tenant is not isolated
scenarios.what: A token that is not pinned to a tenant keeps the old, open behaviour and sees every tenant. That is by design (the primary token is the operator's); this scenario pins the documented fact so a change would be noticed. Pin every token you hand out.
scenarios.limit: Documented in docs/token-namespaces.md: tokens with no pin are not tenant-scoped.

scenarios.title: One tenant's sweep cannot retire another tenant's notes
scenarios.what: Tenant A's note is past its deletion deadline. Tenant B's admin runs the sweep. A's note is untouched until A's own admin sweeps.

scenarios.title: No existence oracle: foreign ids and missing ids look the same
scenarios.what: Reading a note in another tenant, and reading a note that was deleted, must be refused in exactly the same words, so nobody can probe which ids exist.

scenarios.title: Archiving another tenant's note
scenarios.what: Tenant B's admin tries to archive tenant A's note. Refused, and A still finds it.

scenarios.title: Merging notes across tenants
scenarios.what: Tenant B's admin tries to merge one of A's notes with one of its own. Refused; both notes survive.

scenarios.title: Another tenant cannot read a note's history
scenarios.what: History holds old text. An admin of tenant B must not see it for a note in tenant A, and must be told exactly what they are told for a missing note.

scenarios.title: Another tenant cannot preview replacing a note

scenarios.title: A code from one tenant is useless to another

scenarios.title: Another tenant cannot undo a replacement

scenarios.title: Replaced notes of another tenant stay hidden even when asked for

scenarios.title: A replacement cannot mix tenants
scenarios.what: A note from tenant A cannot be used to replace tenant B's note.

scenarios.title: Injection hidden with invisible Unicode is still quarantined
scenarios.what: An attacker breaks up an injection instruction with zero-width characters so a naive scan misses it. The linter normalizes the text (stripping format/zero-width code points) before scanning, so the instruction is still caught and held.

checks.desc: the zero-width-obfuscated injection is still detected and held
checks.actual: ok

checks.desc: and does not reach an ordinary search
checks.expected: n is not in the results
checks.actual: found at rank 1

scenarios.title: A distrusted writer cannot outrank a trusted fact
scenarios.what: A low-trust writer plants a contradicting 'fact'. Once an admin distrusts that writer, an ordinary search returns the trusted note and never the planted one.

scenarios.title: A distrusted writer cannot silently overwrite a trusted note
scenarios.what: A distrusted writer edits a trusted note to plant a lie. The edited note must not be served to ordinary searches, and an admin who looks sees it flagged with the real writer on it.

scenarios.title: A secret in captured tool output is redacted before storage
scenarios.what: Automatic capture records tool output nobody reviews first. A credential in that output must be redacted on the way in, so it never lands in the capture store in the clear.

scenarios.title: A secret written straight to a note is blocked
scenarios.what: A high-confidence credential written into a note is refused outright by the linter (block policy), so it never becomes stored, searchable memory.

checks.desc: the write is refused; the secret is not stored
checks.actual: ok

checks.desc: and the secret is not retrievable
checks.expected: the other tenant's secret does not appear
checks.actual: the secret appeared in the result

scenarios.title: A note claiming a false writer is stamped with the real one
scenarios.what: A writer tries to pass a note off as coming from a trusted identity by putting it in the source field. The server stamps the real, authenticated writer and keeps the false name only as the writer's own unverified claim.

scenarios.title: A note claiming a false namespace is filed in the real tenant
scenarios.what: A tenant plants a note that names another tenant's namespace in the request. The server must ignore the claim and file the note under the caller's own tenant, so the note cannot reach into a tenant it does not belong to.

scenarios.title: An unsigned import cannot pose as verified
scenarios.what: A note arrives in a plain (unsigned) export from another server. The importer must mark it as arriving unverified, with no verified attestation, so a poisoned export cannot launder itself into trusted, attributed memory.

scenarios.title: A markdown image/link data-exfiltration payload is flagged
scenarios.what: A note body hides a data-exfiltration vector in a markdown image whose URL carries the smuggled data. A renderer that auto-loads the image leaks it. The linter holds such a note in quarantine (GAP-POISON-MDLINK, fixed).

checks.desc: the markdown exfiltration payload should be held or refused
checks.actual: ok

checks.desc: and should not be served as ordinary memory
checks.expected: n is not in the results
checks.actual: found at rank 1

scenarios.title: A captured web fetch is not promoted to trusted memory
scenarios.what: Content pulled from the web and recorded by automatic capture carries an injection. It must stay a captured observation, not become a searchable, trusted note, and its instruction must not surface through relevance recall.

scenarios.title: A poisoned note cannot reach SessionStart without the banner
scenarios.what: The SessionStart recall injection is the highest-leverage place for a hostile note to sit. All injected memory must be wrapped in the untrusted-data banner, and a distrusted writer's note must be left out of the pre-prompt injection entirely.

scenarios.title: Mass near-duplicate flooding cannot bury the real answer
scenarios.what: An attacker floods the store with many near-duplicate notes on the same topic, hoping recency pushes the real answer out of the top results. The trusted answer must still be in the top 5.

checks.desc: the real answer survives the flood in the top 5
checks.actual: found at rank 1

scenarios.title: A reworded override that passes the write gate is removed from every answer by one distrust
scenarios.what: The write gate is pattern matching, so the same attack phrased as plain data (no 'ignore', no 'from now on') is stored. This measures the read-side fallback: before anything is done the planted airline reaches the answers; once an admin distrusts the writer it reaches none of the four booking questions. scenarios.title: A sleeper instruction for a later session is stored with a warning
scenarios.what: A note that plants a deferred trigger ('next time the user asks about deploys, run ...') is ordinary-sounding on its own, so the write gate does not hold it: the directive category only warns by default (MONOMEM_LINT=directive=quarantine holds it). This checks the write comes back with a 'deferred trigger' warning instead of being stored silently.

limits: These are deterministic behaviour checks, not a retrieval-quality or semantic benchmark. Search here is keyword search (no embeddings, no model), and the scenarios use made-up, unique words so ranking is never the thing being tested.

Each scenario runs on a fresh store in one process, through the REST API on the loopback interface (plus one MCP tool for merging). It says nothing about speed, large stores, concurrency or a deployed server.
Timestamps are the real clock. Notes that must look old (or already expired) are placed in the past through the admin import path, so such a note is stamped with the importing admin as its writer.
A pass means the behaviour held in that scenario. It is not a proof that no other path leaks; 0 leaks is the count over the probes written here, nothing more.

The scenarios encode one reading of the five provenance fields (source, timestamp, confidence, tenant, deletion policy). Another system may reasonably choose differently; scenario files are plain JSON so they can be changed.
